data.title: AI-SDM Seminar Series: Tom Costello
data.summary:
Correcting Inaccurate Beliefs Using Human-AI Dialogues

Join us for our biweekly seminar series! Lunch is provided for in-person attendees. Please complete the RSVP form to help us with logistics.
data.description:
Abstract
Dialogues with large language models can durably reduce belief in conspiracy theories, a class of beliefs often thought to be resistant to evidence. Further, in field experiments, AI replies on Truth Social and Bluesky reduce later conspiratorial posting. This cuts both ways. When the same models are told to argue that a conspiracy is true, they are about as persuasive as when they argue it is false. In this talk I’ll discuss a set of studies on why these conversations work and what that implies. Finally, I’ll describe a new approach extending this research to climate skepticism. An AI-driven cognitive interview first maps the beliefs underlying a person’s view, and tailored arguments then target those beliefs. This approach outperforms the most effective human-written climate messages, and the advantage persists weeks later. I’ll close by discussing what these results imply for designing the AI systems people increasingly turn to for information.

Speaker Bio
Thomas Costello is an Assistant Professor in Social and Decision Sciences at Carnegie Mellon University. He also holds appointments as Affiliated Faculty at the Human-Computer Interaction Institute at Carnegie Mellon University and is a Research Affiliate at MIT’s Sloan School of Management. His research integrates psychology, political science, and human-computer interaction to examine where our viewpoints come from, how they differ from person to person, and why they change. He also studies the sweeping impacts of artificial intelligence on these belief- and society-related processes.

Speaker Bio
Jeannette Sutton, PhD, is an Associate Professor in the College of Emergency Preparedness, Homeland Security, and Cybersecurity at the University at Albany, SUNY. Dr. Sutton specializes in disaster and risk with a primary focus on online informal communication, and public alerts and warning disseminated via terse messaging channels. Much of her research investigates the evolving role of information and communication technology, including social media and mobile devices, for disaster preparedness, response, and recovery.

Speaker Bio
Aadirupa Saha is an assistant professor at the Department of Computer Science, University of Illinois (UIC), Chicago, since Fall 2025. She is a member of UIC CS Theory group, as well as IDEAL Institute. Previously, she was a research scientist at Apple MLR, broadly working in the area of Machine Learning theory. She completed her postdoc at Microsoft Research (NYC) and PhD from the department of Computer Science, Indian Institute of Science, Bangalore. She was advised by Aditya Gopalan and Chiranjib Bhattacharyya during her PhD and interned at Microsoft Research (In), Inria (Paris), and Google AI (MTV).
